title: The Lion and the Clever Rabbit
preview: A cruel lion terrorised the animals of the forest until they agreed to send one animal each day as his meal. When a small rabbit was chosen, he did not fight with strength. He used calm intelligence, led the lion to a well, and ended the terror by making the lion battle his own reflection.
body: In a great forest lived a powerful lion who hunted whenever he pleased. The animals trembled because no creature was safe. One day, the animals gathered and made a proposal: "O King of the forest, if you stop hunting randomly, we will send one animal to you each day as your meal."

The lion agreed. For many days, one animal went each morning, and the rest of the forest lived in uneasy peace. Then the turn came to a small rabbit. The rabbit knew that running away would only bring danger to everyone, so he began thinking quietly.

He reached the lion very late. The hungry lion roared, "Why are you late?" The rabbit bowed and said, "My lord, I was coming with five other rabbits, but another lion stopped us. He claimed he was the true king of this forest and kept the others."

The lion burned with anger. "Show me this enemy." The rabbit led him to a deep well and said, "He lives inside." The lion looked down and saw his own reflection in the water. Mistaking it for another lion, he roared. The echo roared back.
In fury, the lion leapt into the well to attack his reflection and drowned. The rabbit returned to the animals, and the forest was free.
bodyHi: एक बड़े जंगल में एक शक्तिशाली सिंह रहता था। वह जब चाहे शिकार करता और सभी जीव भय में जीते थे। एक दिन जानवरों ने विनती की कि यदि वह बिना कारण शिकार न करे, तो वे रोज़ एक जीव उसके भोजन के लिए भेजेंगे।
सिंह मान गया। कई दिनों तक यह चलता रहा। फिर एक छोटे खरगोश की बारी आई। खरगोश ने सोचा कि भागने से सबका संकट बढ़ेगा, इसलिए उसने बुद्धि से उपाय खोजा।
वह सिंह के पास बहुत देर से पहुँचा। सिंह गरजा, "इतनी देर क्यों?" खरगोश ने कहा, "महाराज, मैं पाँच खरगोशों के साथ आ रहा था, पर एक और सिंह ने हमें रोक लिया। वह स्वयं को इस जंगल का राजा बताता है।"
सिंह क्रोध से भर गया। खरगोश उसे एक गहरे कुएँ के पास ले गया और बोला, "वह इसी में रहता है।" सिंह ने पानी में अपना प्रतिबिंब देखा और उसे दूसरा सिंह समझ लिया।
क्रोध में सिंह कुएँ में कूद पड़ा और डूब गया। खरगोश लौट आया और जंगल भय से मुक्त हो गया।
phal: Wisdom can defeat force when the mind remains calm. The story teaches that panic strengthens danger, while observation and strategy can protect the whole community.
phalHi: शांत बुद्धि बल से बड़ी होती है। संकट में घबराने के बजाय समझ, धैर्य और युक्ति से काम लेना चाहिए।

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
preview: A monkey shared sweet fruits with a crocodile and treated him as a friend. But the crocodile, pressured by his wife, tried to deceive the monkey. In the middle of the river, the monkey discovered the danger and saved himself through presence of mind.
body: On the bank of a river stood a fruit tree where a cheerful monkey lived. Every day he ate sweet fruits and watched the river flow. One day, a crocodile came near the tree. The monkey, generous by nature, offered him some fruits.

The crocodile enjoyed them and began visiting often. A friendship grew between the two. The crocodile also carried fruits home to his wife. After tasting them, she became greedy and thought, "If the fruits are so sweet, the monkey who eats them daily must have an even sweeter heart."
She asked her husband to bring the monkey to her. The crocodile was troubled but gave in to her demand. He invited the monkey to visit his home across the river and offered to carry him on his back.

Halfway across the river, the crocodile confessed the truth: his wife wanted the monkey's heart. The monkey did not panic. He said, "Friend, why did you not tell me earlier? I left my heart on the tree. Take me back and I will bring it."
The foolish crocodile turned back. As soon as they reached the tree, the monkey jumped to safety and said, "No one leaves their heart behind. A friend who betrays trust cannot be trusted again."
bodyHi: एक नदी के किनारे मीठे फलों का पेड़ था, जिस पर एक बंदर रहता था। एक दिन एक मगरमच्छ वहाँ आया। बंदर ने उदारता से उसे फल दिए।
मगरमच्छ रोज़ आने लगा और दोनों में मित्रता हो गई। वह फल अपनी पत्नी के लिए भी ले जाता था। पत्नी ने सोचा कि जो बंदर रोज़ इतने मीठे फल खाता है, उसका हृदय भी मीठा होगा।
उसने मगरमच्छ से बंदर को लाने को कहा। मगरमच्छ ने बंदर को अपने घर चलने का निमंत्रण दिया और पीठ पर बैठाकर नदी पार कराने लगा।
नदी के बीच मगरमच्छ ने सच बता दिया। बंदर घबराया नहीं। उसने कहा, "मित्र, तुमने पहले क्यों नहीं बताया? मेरा हृदय तो पेड़ पर ही रह गया है। मुझे वापस ले चलो।"
मगरमच्छ उसे वापस ले आया। बंदर तुरंत पेड़ पर चढ़ गया और बोला, "हृदय कोई पेड़ पर नहीं छोड़ता। जो मित्र विश्वास तोड़े, उससे सावधान रहना चाहिए।"
phal: Generosity needs discernment. The story teaches kindness, but also the importance of recognising betrayal and protecting oneself without hatred.
phalHi: उदारता के साथ विवेक भी आवश्यक है। मित्रता विश्वास पर टिकती है; छल करने वाले से सावधान रहना चाहिए।

title: The Blue Jackal
preview: A jackal fell into a dyer's vat and emerged blue. The forest animals, frightened by his strange colour, accepted him as a divine king. For a while he enjoyed power, but when he forgot himself and howled with other jackals, the truth was revealed.
body: A hungry jackal once wandered into a town looking for food. Dogs chased him through the streets, and in panic he jumped into a large vat in a dyer's courtyard. The vat was full of deep blue dye.

When he climbed out, his fur had become a strange blue colour. Returning to the forest, he saw that the animals were frightened by his unusual appearance. The jackal quickly understood the opportunity.

"Do not fear," he declared. "The gods have sent me as your king." The animals believed him. Lions, tigers, elephants, and deer all bowed before the blue creature. The jackal enjoyed royal food and honour.
But he grew arrogant and forgot his old companions. One evening, a pack of jackals howled in the distance. Hearing them, the blue jackal could not control himself. He lifted his head and howled back.
The animals immediately recognised him. "He is only a jackal in disguise," they said. His false kingship ended at once.
bodyHi: एक भूखा सियार भोजन की तलाश में नगर में गया। कुत्तों ने उसे दौड़ाया और घबराकर वह रंगरेज़ के नीले रंग के बड़े पात्र में कूद गया।
जब वह बाहर निकला, तो उसका शरीर नीला हो चुका था। जंगल में लौटकर उसने देखा कि जानवर उसके विचित्र रूप से डर रहे हैं। उसने तुरंत अवसर समझ लिया।
उसने कहा, "डरो मत। देवताओं ने मुझे तुम्हारा राजा बनाकर भेजा है।" सभी जानवरों ने उसे राजा मान लिया।
कुछ समय तक वह सम्मान और सुख भोगता रहा। पर एक दिन दूर से सियारों की आवाज़ आई। वह स्वयं को रोक न सका और सियारों की तरह हुआँ-हुआँ करने लगा।
जानवरों ने पहचान लिया कि वह कोई दिव्य प्राणी नहीं, साधारण सियार है। उसका झूठा राज्य समाप्त हो गया।
phal: False identity cannot survive for long. The story teaches humility, authenticity, and the danger of gaining respect through deception.
phalHi: झूठी पहचान अधिक समय तक नहीं टिकती। सम्मान छल से नहीं, सत्य और विनम्रता से मिलना चाहिए।

title: The Brahmin and the Three Crooks
preview: A Brahmin carried a goat for sacrifice when three crooks planned to steal it. They did not use force. Each one met him separately and called the goat a dog. Hearing the same lie again and again, the Brahmin began doubting his own eyes.
body: A Brahmin once received a healthy goat as a gift and carried it home on his shoulders. Three crooks saw him and wanted the goat, but they knew they could not snatch it openly.
The first crook came along the road and said, "Revered sir, why are you carrying a dirty dog on your shoulders?" The Brahmin was offended. "This is a goat, not a dog," he replied and walked on.
After some distance, the second crook appeared and said with surprise, "O learned one, why would a Brahmin carry a dead calf?" The Brahmin became uneasy but continued walking.
Then the third crook met him and laughed, "What a strange sight. A holy man carrying a dog!" Now the Brahmin was shaken. "If three people have said this, perhaps something is wrong," he thought.
Fearing impurity, he threw the goat aside and hurried away. The three crooks collected the goat and laughed at how repetition had defeated clear seeing.
bodyHi: एक ब्राह्मण को उपहार में एक स्वस्थ बकरी मिली। वह उसे कंधे पर रखकर घर जा रहा था। तीन ठगों ने बकरी देखी और उसे चुराने की योजना बनाई।
पहला ठग रास्ते में आया और बोला, "महाराज, आप यह गंदा कुत्ता कंधे पर क्यों उठाए हैं?" ब्राह्मण ने कहा, "यह बकरी है, कुत्ता नहीं।"
थोड़ी दूर पर दूसरा ठग मिला। उसने कहा, "आश्चर्य है, एक विद्वान ब्राह्मण मरा हुआ बछड़ा लेकर जा रहा है।" ब्राह्मण बेचैन हुआ, पर आगे चलता रहा।
फिर तीसरा ठग आया और हँसकर बोला, "कैसा विचित्र दृश्य है, एक ब्राह्मण कुत्ता उठाए जा रहा है।" अब ब्राह्मण डर गया।
उसने सोचा, "यदि तीन लोग ऐसा कह रहे हैं, तो शायद मेरी दृष्टि भ्रमित है।" उसने बकरी छोड़ दी और चला गया। ठगों ने बकरी उठा ली।
phal: Repeated falsehood can disturb weak conviction. The story teaches that one must examine facts directly and not surrender judgment merely because many voices repeat the same claim.
phalHi: बार-बार बोला गया झूठ भी कमजोर विश्वास को हिला सकता है। सत्य को स्वयं देखकर परखना चाहिए।

title: The Crows and the Cobra
preview: A pair of crows lived happily in a tree, but a cobra in the hollow below ate their eggs again and again. Unable to defeat the snake directly, the crows sought advice from a wise jackal and used the king's own guards to remove the danger.
body: A crow and his mate built their nest high in a tree. Below the same tree lived a cobra in a hollow. Whenever the crows laid eggs, the cobra climbed up and ate them.
The mother crow wept, and the father crow wanted to fight, but the cobra was too strong. They went to a wise jackal and asked for help.
The jackal said, "Do not fight strength with weakness. Use the strength of one power against another. Fly to the palace, take something precious, and drop it near the cobra's hole."

The crows flew to the palace garden, where the queen had removed her necklace while bathing. One crow picked it up and flew slowly so the guards could follow. Then he dropped it into the cobra's hollow.
The guards reached the tree, saw the necklace inside the hole, and dug it out. When the cobra emerged, they killed it. The crows were safe and raised their young in peace.
bodyHi: एक कौआ और उसकी पत्नी पेड़ पर रहते थे। उसी पेड़ के नीचे एक खोखले में साँप रहता था। जब भी कौए अंडे देते, साँप उन्हें खा जाता।
कौवी दुखी रहती थी। कौआ लड़ना चाहता था, पर साँप शक्तिशाली था। दोनों एक बुद्धिमान सियार के पास गए।
सियार ने कहा, "कमज़ोरी से शक्ति पर सीधा आक्रमण मत करो। एक शक्ति का उपयोग दूसरी शक्ति के विरुद्ध करो। महल से कोई कीमती वस्तु लाकर साँप के बिल में गिरा दो।"
कौए महल के बगीचे में गए। रानी का हार वहाँ रखा था। एक कौआ हार उठाकर धीरे-धीरे उड़ा ताकि सैनिक पीछा करें। फिर उसने हार साँप के बिल में गिरा दिया।
सैनिक आए, बिल खोदा, हार निकाला और साँप को मार दिया। कौए सुरक्षित हो गए।
phal: When direct force is impossible, wise strategy protects life. The story teaches measured action, patience, and using the right help instead of reacting blindly.
phalHi: जब सीधा बल काम न करे, तो युक्ति और सही सहायता से संकट दूर किया जा सकता है।

title: The Talkative Tortoise
preview: Two swans tried to save their tortoise friend from a drying lake by carrying him with a stick. There was only one condition: he must keep his mouth shut. But when people mocked him from below, he could not resist speaking.
body: A tortoise lived in a lake with two swans as his close friends. When the lake began drying, the swans decided to fly to another lake and take the tortoise with them.
They brought a strong stick and said, "Hold the middle of this stick in your mouth. We will hold both ends and fly. But you must not speak until we land."
The tortoise agreed. The swans lifted him into the sky. People below looked up and shouted, "Look at that foolish tortoise flying between two birds!"
The tortoise became angry. He opened his mouth to reply, "I am not foolish!" The moment he spoke, he lost his grip and fell.
The swans grieved for their friend. His life could have been saved by silence, but his need to answer insult became stronger than wisdom.
bodyHi: एक कछुआ दो हंसों का मित्र था। जब झील सूखने लगी, तो हंसों ने उसे दूसरी झील ले जाने का उपाय किया।
उन्होंने एक मजबूत लकड़ी लाई और कहा, "तुम इसे बीच से मुँह में पकड़ो। हम दोनों सिरों को पकड़कर उड़ेंगे। पर जब तक उतरें नहीं, बोलना मत।"
कछुआ मान गया। हंस उसे लेकर उड़ चले। नीचे लोगों ने देखकर कहा, "देखो, मूर्ख कछुआ पक्षियों के बीच उड़ रहा है!"
कछुआ क्रोधित हो गया। वह बोला, "मैं मूर्ख नहीं हूँ!" बोलते ही लकड़ी छूट गई और वह नीचे गिर पड़ा।
हंस दुखी हुए। मौन से उसकी रक्षा हो सकती थी, पर अपमान का उत्तर देने की इच्छा बुद्धि से बड़ी हो गई।
phal: Not every insult deserves an answer. The story teaches restraint in speech and the power of silence when safety, dignity, or purpose depends on it.
phalHi: हर अपमान का उत्तर देना आवश्यक नहीं। कई बार मौन ही रक्षा और बुद्धिमत्ता है।

title: The Loyal Mongoose
preview: A family kept a mongoose who loved their baby like his own. One day the mother returned home and saw blood on the mongoose's mouth. Without looking inside, she assumed the worst. Only later did she see the snake he had killed to protect the child.
body: A Brahmin family kept a young mongoose in their home. The mongoose grew up with their baby and loved the child deeply. The mother trusted him, but a small doubt remained in her heart because he was still a wild creature.

One day she left the baby sleeping and went to fetch water. While she was gone, a snake entered the house and moved toward the cradle. The mongoose attacked the snake and killed it after a fierce struggle.

When the mother returned, the mongoose ran to greet her with blood on his mouth. Without entering the room or checking the child, she cried, "You have killed my baby!" In blind fear, she struck him down.
Then she rushed inside and found her child safe, sleeping peacefully. Beside the cradle lay the dead snake. The mongoose had protected the baby with his life.
The mother wept bitterly, but regret could not undo the act done in haste.
bodyHi: एक ब्राह्मण परिवार ने घर में नेवला पाला था। वह बच्चे के साथ बड़ा हुआ और उससे बहुत प्रेम करता था। माँ को उस पर विश्वास था, पर मन में थोड़ा संदेह भी रहता था।
एक दिन माँ पानी लेने गई और बच्चा सो रहा था। तभी घर में साँप घुस आया और पालने की ओर बढ़ा। नेवले ने साँप से लड़कर उसे मार दिया।
माँ लौटी तो नेवला खून लगे मुँह से उसके पास आया। बिना भीतर जाकर देखे, माँ चिल्लाई, "तूने मेरे बच्चे को मार दिया!" भय में उसने नेवले को मार डाला।
फिर वह भीतर गई। बच्चा सुरक्षित सो रहा था और पास में मरा हुआ साँप पड़ा था। नेवले ने बच्चे की रक्षा की थी।
माँ पछताई, पर जल्दबाज़ी में किया गया काम वापस नहीं हो सकता था।
phal: Hasty judgment can destroy what loyalty has protected. The story teaches verification before action, especially when fear or anger is strong.
phalHi: जल्दबाज़ी में किया गया निर्णय बड़ा अनर्थ कर सकता है। भय या क्रोध में काम करने से पहले सत्य अवश्य जाँचना चाहिए।

title: The Foolish Friend
preview: A king trusted a loyal monkey who loved him deeply but lacked judgment. When a fly sat on the sleeping king, the monkey tried to protect him with a sword. Loyalty without wisdom became dangerous.
body: A king had a pet monkey who was devoted to him. The monkey stayed near the king day and night, waving a fan, guarding the room, and trying to serve with complete loyalty.
One afternoon, while the king slept, a fly kept landing on his chest. The monkey chased it away again and again, but the fly returned. In anger, the monkey picked up the king's sword.

When the fly landed once more, the monkey struck with all his strength. The fly escaped, but the sword wounded the king. The court learned that affection without judgment can be more dangerous than open hostility.
phal: Choose companions for wisdom as well as affection. Good intention cannot replace good judgment.
phalHi: मित्रता में प्रेम के साथ विवेक भी आवश्यक है। केवल नीयत अच्छी होना पर्याप्त नहीं।

title: The Two Fish and the Frog
preview: Two clever fish argued about what to do when fishermen planned to drain their pond. A frog acted immediately and moved away. The fish delayed, debated, and paid the price.
body: In a pond lived two proud fish and a practical frog. One evening they heard fishermen say, "Tomorrow we will cast our nets here." The frog told the fish, "We must leave before sunrise."
One fish said, "I know many tricks." The other said, "I can escape any net." The frog did not argue. He carried his family through a wet channel to another pond that night.
The next morning the fishermen came. The fish tried their clever methods, but the nets were too many. The frog survived because he respected danger before it arrived.
phal: Timely action is better than clever excuses. Wisdom means moving before the crisis closes every path.
phalHi: समय पर किया गया काम सबसे बड़ी बुद्धिमानी है। संकट आने के बाद चतुराई भी कम पड़ सकती है।

title: The Bird with Two Heads
preview: A strange bird had two heads but one body. One head ate sweet fruit and refused to share. The other, filled with resentment, ate poison. Both perished because they forgot they shared one life.
body: A rare bird lived near a river. It had two heads but only one body. One day, the first head found a delicious fruit and ate it happily.
The second head asked for a share. The first replied, "We have one stomach, so why should it matter who eats?" The second head felt insulted and carried resentment for days.
Later, the second head found a poisonous fruit and ate it deliberately. The poison entered the one body they shared, and both heads died. Division within one body destroys all.
phal: Family, community, and nation share one body. Harm done in resentment returns to everyone.
phalHi: परिवार और समाज एक शरीर की तरह हैं। ईर्ष्या से किया गया नुकसान सबको चोट पहुँचाता है।

title: The Crane and the Crab
preview: An old crane pretended to help fish move to a safer pond, but he ate them one by one. A crab discovered the truth and saved himself by refusing blind trust.
body: An old crane could no longer catch fish easily. He stood sadly beside a pond and told the fish, "This pond will dry soon. I can carry you to a larger lake."
The frightened fish trusted him. Each day he carried one fish away, but instead of taking it to another lake, he ate it on a rock. At last a crab asked to be carried too.
From the crane's neck, the crab saw the bones of the fish below. He tightened his claws around the crane's throat and saved himself. The pond learned that fear makes false helpers powerful.
phal: Do not accept help that cannot be verified. A calm mind checks both the promise and the path.
phalHi: भय में किया गया अंधा विश्वास खतरनाक है। सहायता स्वीकार करने से पहले सत्य जाँचें।

title: The Merchant and the Iron Balance
preview: A merchant left an iron balance with a friend. When he returned, the friend claimed rats had eaten it. The merchant answered dishonesty with a clever lesson.
body: A merchant stored a heavy iron balance with a friend before leaving town. When he returned and asked for it, the friend lied, "Rats ate your balance."
The merchant understood the deceit but remained calm. Later he took the friend's young son for a walk and hid him safely. When asked about the child, he said, "A hawk carried him away."
The friend cried, "How can a hawk carry a boy?" The merchant replied, "In a city where rats eat iron, hawks may carry children." The friend returned the balance, and the child was returned safely.
phal: Dishonesty often exposes itself when mirrored back. Justice needs intelligence, not uncontrolled anger.
phalHi: झूठ को कभी-कभी उसी के तर्क से दिखाना पड़ता है। न्याय के लिए बुद्धि चाहिए, क्रोध नहीं।

title: The Lion, the Mouse, and the Cat
preview: A lion could not sleep because a mouse nibbled his mane. He brought a cat to solve the problem. When the mouse vanished, the lion forgot the cat too.
body: A lion was troubled by a tiny mouse who nibbled his mane while he slept. The lion could not catch such a small creature, so he invited a cat to live nearby.
The cat's presence frightened the mouse into hiding. The lion slept peacefully. For some time he fed the cat well and treated her as useful.
When the mouse no longer appeared, the lion stopped feeding the cat. The cat left hungry, thinking, "Some rulers value service only while the danger is visible."
phal: Do not forget those who protect you after the problem disappears. Gratitude must outlive usefulness.
phalHi: संकट दूर होने के बाद मदद करने वाले को भूलना कृतघ्नता है। उपकार को याद रखना चाहिए।

title: The Jackal and the Drum
preview: A jackal heard a terrifying sound in an abandoned battlefield. Instead of running forever, he investigated and found only an empty drum struck by branches.
body: A hungry jackal wandered across an old battlefield. Suddenly he heard a deep booming sound. It echoed through the trees and filled him with fear.
At first he wanted to flee, but hunger made him pause. "A sound alone cannot harm me," he thought. He moved carefully toward it.
He found a large empty drum. Branches struck it whenever the wind blew. The jackal laughed and learned that many fears are loud because they are hollow.
phal: Investigate fear before surrendering to it. Noise is not always danger.
phalHi: डर को जाँचें। हर ऊँची आवाज़ वास्तविक संकट नहीं होती।

title: The Dove King and the Net
preview: A flock of doves was trapped in a hunter's net. Their king told them not to panic. Together they lifted the net and flew to a mouse friend who freed them.
body: A hunter spread grain under a net. A flock of doves landed to eat and were trapped. Each bird struggled alone, making the net tighter.
Their king said, "Do not pull separately. Fly together." At his signal, all the doves beat their wings in one rhythm and lifted the entire net into the sky.
They flew to a mouse who was the king's friend. The mouse cut the knots and freed them. Unity turned a trap into a burden they could carry away.
phal: A united group can lift what defeats each person alone. Panic separates; rhythm saves.
phalHi: एकता से वह भार भी उठ जाता है जो अकेले असंभव लगता है।

title: The Mice and the Elephants
preview: A herd of elephants crushed a city of mice without noticing. The mouse king asked for mercy. Later, when hunters trapped the elephants, the tiny mice repaid kindness.
body: A herd of elephants passed daily through a ruined city where thousands of mice lived. Many mice were crushed under their feet. The mouse king respectfully asked the elephant king to use another path.
The elephant king agreed. Some elephants laughed, "What help can mice ever give us?" But the king replied, "No creature is too small for respect."
Later hunters trapped the elephants with ropes. The mouse king brought his people, and they gnawed through the ropes. The elephants were freed by those they had once spared.
phal: Respect the small. A life protected today may protect you tomorrow.
phalHi: छोटे को भी सम्मान दें। आज जिसे बचाएँगे, कल वही आपका सहारा बन सकता है।

title: The Jackal and the Sour Grapes
preview: A hungry jackal tried again and again to reach grapes hanging high above him. When he failed, he walked away saying they were sour anyway.
body: A hungry jackal saw ripe grapes hanging from a vine. He jumped once, twice, and many times, but the grapes remained just beyond his reach.
Tired and embarrassed, he looked around to see if anyone had watched him fail. Then he lifted his nose and said, "Those grapes are probably sour."
He walked away still hungry. The grapes had not changed; only his story about them had changed to protect his pride.
phal: Do not insult what you failed to reach. Honest effort teaches more than defensive pride.
phalHi: जिसे पा न सकें, उसे तुच्छ कहना अहंकार है। असफलता को ईमानदारी से स्वीकारना सीख है।

title: The Ass in the Tiger Skin
preview: A washerman dressed his donkey in a tiger skin so it could graze freely. Everyone feared it until the donkey heard another donkey and brayed.
body: A washerman covered his donkey with a tiger skin and let it graze in other people's fields at night. The farmers saw the shape and ran away in fear.
The donkey enjoyed the rich crops and grew fat. But one night he heard another donkey braying from far away.
Forgetting the disguise, he brayed loudly in answer. The farmers recognised him at once. A borrowed appearance cannot hide one's nature for long.
phal: Outer disguise cannot replace inner growth. Character eventually speaks.
phalHi: बाहरी रूप भीतर की प्रकृति को अधिक समय तक नहीं छिपा सकता।

title: The Greedy Jackal
preview: A jackal found a hunter, a deer, and a boar dead in one place. Instead of eating steadily, he wanted to begin with the bowstring. His greed ended his feast before it began.
body: A jackal found a strange scene: a hunter, a deer, and a wild boar all dead after a struggle. He rejoiced, thinking he had food for many days.
Instead of eating carefully, he noticed the hunter's bowstring and thought, "Let me begin with this small strip first." He bit into it greedily.
The tight bow snapped back and struck him fatally. Surrounded by abundance, he was destroyed by impatience over a small thing.
phal: Greed makes abundance unsafe. Contentment protects what desire wastes.
phalHi: लालच बहुत कुछ होते हुए भी विनाश ला सकता है। संतोष रक्षा करता है।

title: The Heron Who Spoke of Renunciation
preview: A heron pretended he had given up eating fish and spoke like a saint. The fish trusted his words, but his actions revealed his hunger.
body: An old heron stood silently by a pond. When the fish asked why he did not hunt, he sighed, "I have renounced violence. I only grieve because this pond will soon dry."
The fish begged for help. The heron offered to carry them to another lake. One by one, he carried them away and ate them behind a rock.
A cautious crab asked to see the route. When he saw bones near the rock, he understood. He escaped and warned the pond. Holy words without honest conduct are dangerous.
phal: Do not trust spiritual language without truthful action. Dharma is proved by conduct.
phalHi: धर्म की बातें तभी सच्ची हैं जब आचरण भी सच्चा हो।

title: The Sparrow and the Elephant
preview: An arrogant elephant crushed a sparrow's eggs. The tiny bird gathered friends: a woodpecker, a fly, and a frog. Together they humbled the giant.
body: A sparrow had a nest with eggs on a tree branch. An arrogant elephant, drunk with power, shook the tree for sport and broke the eggs.
The sparrow wept but did not give up. She asked a woodpecker, a fly, and a frog for help. Each friend had a small skill.
The fly distracted the elephant, the woodpecker hurt his eyes, and the frog croaked near a pit so he walked toward the sound and fell. Small allies, united by justice, defeated careless power.
phal: The weak are not helpless when they organise with wisdom. Skill, timing, and friendship balance strength.
phalHi: छोटे भी संगठित होकर बड़े अन्याय का सामना कर सकते हैं।

title: The King and the Wise Minister
preview: A king grew angry whenever advice displeased him. His minister taught him that unpleasant truth is often the medicine that protects a throne.
body: A king loved praise. Courtiers quickly learned to agree with everything he said. Only one old minister continued to speak honestly.

When the king became angry, the minister said, "A mirror does not insult the face. It only shows what is there." The king dismissed him but soon made a costly decision because no one dared correct him.
Realising the danger of flattery, the king called the minister back. From then on, he treated honest criticism as protection, not disrespect.
phal: Leadership needs truth more than praise. Wise counsel may feel sharp because it cuts away error.
phalHi: नेतृत्व को प्रशंसा से अधिक सत्य की आवश्यकता होती है।

title: The Owls and the Crows
preview: The crows could not defeat the owls in direct battle. One crow pretended to defect, learned the enemy's weakness, and used patience instead of panic.
body: The owls and crows were enemies. The owls attacked at night, when the crows could not see. Many crows wanted immediate revenge, but their elder advised strategy.
One crow pretended to be rejected by his own people and took shelter near the owls. Slowly he gained their trust and learned where they slept during the day.
When the time was right, he returned to the crows. They blocked the owls' cave with dry grass and smoke. Strategy succeeded where rage would have failed.
phal: Know the nature of the problem before acting. Timing and intelligence can defeat repeated loss.
phalHi: किसी भी समस्या पर काम करने से पहले उसकी प्रकृति समझें। समय और बुद्धि से विजय मिलती है।

title: The Rabbits and the Moon Lake
preview: Elephants trampled the rabbits while searching for water. A wise rabbit protected his people by speaking to the elephant king in the name of the moon.
body: During a drought, elephants came to a lake where rabbits lived. Their heavy feet crushed many burrows. The rabbits feared extinction.
A wise rabbit approached the elephant king at night and said, "This lake belongs to the Moon. Your herd has disturbed his children." He showed the moon's reflection trembling in the water.
The elephant king believed the moon was displeased and led his herd away. The rabbits survived because one voice spoke with courage and imagination.
phal: When direct power is absent, symbolic intelligence can protect the vulnerable.
phalHi: सीधा बल न हो तो प्रतीक, भाषा और बुद्धि से भी रक्षा की जा सकती है।

title: The Bird with Golden Droppings
preview: A hunter found a bird whose droppings turned to gold. A king and minister argued without wisdom, and greed made everyone lose what fortune had given.
body: A hunter caught a strange bird whose droppings turned into gold. Amazed, he feared keeping it secretly and presented it to the king.
The minister laughed, "No bird can produce gold. This is a trick." Without testing properly, the king released the bird.
The bird flew to a branch, dropped gold once more, and said, "First the hunter was foolish, then the minister, then the king." Fortune leaves when judgment is absent.
phal: Rejecting evidence without inquiry is also foolishness. Test before you dismiss.
phalHi: बिना जाँच के अस्वीकार करना भी मूर्खता है। प्रमाण को परखें।

title: The Weaver Who Pretended to Be Vishnu
preview: A weaver used a disguise to impress a princess. For a while illusion worked, but fear of real danger forced him to become braver than his lie.
body: A poor weaver loved a princess and knew he could never meet her honestly. With a friend's help, he made a wooden Garuda and dressed as Vishnu to visit her at night.
The princess believed him divine. But when the kingdom faced war, the king begged the "Lord" to protect them. The weaver trembled because his disguise had become a public burden.
Ashamed yet trapped, he went to battle and fought with unexpected courage. The story warns that deception may bring a role one is not ready to carry.
phal: False elevation creates real responsibility. Do not pretend to be what you are unwilling to become.
phalHi: झूठी ऊँचाई सच्ची जिम्मेदारी बन जाती है। जो बनना न चाहें, उसका ढोंग न करें।

title: The Four Friends
preview: A deer, crow, mouse, and tortoise proved that different strengths become powerful when joined by loyalty.
body: A deer, a crow, a mouse, and a tortoise became close friends. Each was different: one swift, one watchful, one able to cut, and one steady.
When a hunter trapped the deer in a net, the crow found him, the mouse cut the net, and the tortoise waited nearby. Later, when the tortoise was caught, the others worked together again.
The deer pretended to be dead, the hunter put down the tortoise, and the mouse freed him. Friendship turned separate abilities into shared safety.
phal: A good circle does not require everyone to be the same. Different strengths, joined by trust, create resilience.
phalHi: सच्ची मित्रता में सबका समान होना जरूरी नहीं। अलग-अलग गुण मिलकर शक्ति बनते हैं।

title: The Cat as Judge
preview: A partridge and a hare argued over a home and asked an old cat to judge. The cat spoke softly about dharma until both came close enough to be eaten.
body: A partridge returned to his old nest and found a hare living there. They argued over ownership and decided to ask someone wise to judge.
They saw an old cat sitting like a saint by the river. The cat spoke of non-violence and justice, saying, "Come closer; my ears are weak."
Trusting his gentle words, both came near. The cat seized them. The dispute ended not through justice but through choosing a judge without character.
phal: Do not take disputes to someone who benefits from both sides losing.
phalHi: जिसे दोनों पक्षों के नष्ट होने में लाभ हो, उसे न्यायाधीश न बनाएं।

title: The Donkey and the Jackal
preview: A donkey and a jackal raided a cucumber field at night. The donkey insisted on singing. His voice brought the farmer.
body: A donkey and a jackal entered a cucumber field at night. They ate well in silence until the donkey felt joyful and wanted to sing.
The jackal warned, "This is not a concert hall. If you sing, the farmer will come." The donkey ignored him and brayed loudly.
The farmer woke and beat the donkey. The jackal escaped, thinking, "Pleasure without self-control invites punishment."
phal: There is a time and place for expression. Joy needs discretion.
phalHi: हर अभिव्यक्ति का समय और स्थान होता है। आनंद में भी विवेक रखें।

title: The Snake Who Carried Frogs
preview: An old snake pretended to be cursed to carry frogs on his back. The frog king enjoyed the ride until the snake slowly ate his people.
body: An old snake could not hunt well. He told the frogs, "I am cursed to serve frogs as a carrier." The frog king was delighted and rode on his back.
The snake moved slowly and gained trust. Then he said, "I am weak from hunger. May I eat one frog a day?" The proud king agreed carelessly.
Soon the pond grew empty. The king realised too late that comfort bought with another's suffering eventually reaches one's own door.
phal: Leaders must not trade their people's safety for personal comfort.
phalHi: नेता को अपने सुख के लिए प्रजा की सुरक्षा से समझौता नहीं करना चाहिए।

title: The Camel with the Bell
preview: A camel loved the bell around his neck and wandered proudly away from the herd. The sound that made him feel special helped predators find him.
body: A merchant tied a bell around one camel's neck to identify him. The camel grew proud of the sound and began walking apart from the herd.
Other camels warned him, "Stay with us. The bell can guide danger too." But he liked feeling special and wandered alone.
A lion heard the bell from far away and followed it. The camel learned too late that vanity can announce weakness.
phal: What makes us noticeable should not make us careless. Distinction without discipline invites risk.
phalHi: विशेष दिखना अच्छा है, पर सावधानी छोड़ना खतरनाक है।

title: The Potter Mistaken for a Warrior
preview: A potter had a scar from falling on broken pots. A king mistook it for a battle wound and honoured him as a hero. Truth emerged when real war came.
body: A potter once fell on broken pots and received a deep scar on his forehead. Years later, a king saw the scar and assumed he was a brave soldier.
The potter was given honour in the army. He enjoyed the respect but did not explain the truth. Then war approached, and the king asked him to lead fighters.
Terrified, the potter confessed. The king said, "A scar is not courage." Titles gained by misunderstanding cannot stand before real duty.
phal: Reputation without capacity becomes a burden. Be honest before expectation becomes danger.
phalHi: योग्यता बिना प्रतिष्ठा बोझ बन जाती है। अपेक्षा बढ़ने से पहले सच बोलें।

title: The Brahmin Who Built Castles in the Air
titleHi: हवा में महल बनाने वाला ब्राह्मण
preview: A Brahmin imagined wealth from a pot of flour. In his daydream, he kicked out at an imaginary child and broke the pot that held his real food.
body: A poor Brahmin received a pot of flour and hung it above his bed. Looking at it, he imagined selling it, buying goats, becoming rich, marrying, and having children.
In the dream, he imagined scolding a disobedient child. He kicked his foot to show authority.
His foot struck the real pot. It shattered, and the flour spilled everywhere. His future palace vanished because he neglected the present vessel.
phal: Planning is useful; fantasy without action destroys what is already in hand.
phalHi: योजना ठीक है, पर कर्महीन कल्पना वर्तमान साधन भी नष्ट कर देती है।

title: The Hare Who Protected the Lake
preview: A small hare saved his whole colony by approaching the elephant king with dignity and a story the king could understand.
body: When elephants damaged the hares' home near a lake, the hares gathered in fear. One small hare volunteered to speak to the elephant king.
He climbed a rock and said, "I am a messenger of the Moon, whose lake you have disturbed." He spoke calmly, without insult or panic.
The elephant king saw the moon reflected in the water and accepted the warning. The hare saved many lives by using language the powerful would respect.
phal: Communication matters. The right words, spoken calmly, can turn power away from harm.
phalHi: सही भाषा और शांत साहस से बड़ी शक्ति को भी अहिंसा की ओर मोड़ा जा सकता है।

title: Dharmabuddhi and Papabuddhi
preview: Two friends hid money under a tree. One stole it and tried to make the tree itself witness against the innocent friend.
body: Two friends, Dharmabuddhi and Papabuddhi, earned money together and hid it under a tree. Later Papabuddhi secretly stole the money.
When they returned, he accused Dharmabuddhi. He even hid his father inside the hollow tree to speak as a false witness.
The judge ordered smoke into the hollow, and the hidden father came out coughing. The lie was exposed. A false witness traps the one who arranges it.
phal: Truth may be delayed, but elaborate lies create more doors through which truth can enter.
phalHi: सत्य देर से आए, पर जटिल झूठ स्वयं अपने रास्ते खोल देता है।

title: The Sage and the Mouse
preview: A sage transformed a frightened mouse into stronger forms, but fear remained. When pride arose, the sage returned him to his true nature.
body: A sage rescued a mouse from a hawk. Seeing its fear, he transformed it into a cat, then a dog, then a tiger so it could feel safe.
But each new form brought a new fear. Finally, as a tiger, the creature grew proud and thought of attacking the sage himself.
The sage understood and turned him back into a mouse. Outer power had changed, but inner nature had not been purified.
phal: Transformation must happen inside, not only in status or strength.
phalHi: सच्चा परिवर्तन भीतर होता है, केवल रूप या शक्ति बदलने से नहीं।

title: The Lion and the Bull
preview: A lion and bull became friends, but jealous jackals poisoned their trust. Both suffered because they believed whispers over direct conversation.
body: A strong bull became separated from his caravan and lived near a forest. His deep bellow frightened the lion king until they met and became friends.
Two jackals who had lost influence grew jealous. They whispered to the lion that the bull planned rebellion and told the bull that the lion meant to kill him.
Instead of speaking directly, both believed suspicion. Their friendship collapsed in conflict. The jackals gained from the silence between friends.
phal: Do not let third voices replace direct conversation with those you trust.
phalHi: विश्वास वाले संबंधों में तीसरे की बात से पहले सीधा संवाद करें।

title: The Monk and the Jackal
preview: A monk saved a jackal from a hunter. The jackal promised gratitude, but when temptation came, its old habits returned.
body: A monk once hid a jackal from hunters. The jackal bowed and promised, "I will always remember your kindness."
Some days later, the jackal found the monk's food bowl unattended. Hunger and habit overcame gratitude, and he dragged the food away.
The monk saw him and sighed, "A saved life is not always a changed heart." Gratitude must be practised, not merely spoken.
phal: Kindness is noble, but transformation belongs to the receiver. Watch actions, not promises.
phalHi: करुणा श्रेष्ठ है, पर परिवर्तन पाने वाले के अभ्यास पर निर्भर है। वचन नहीं, कर्म देखें।

title: The Scholars Who Made a Lion
preview: Three scholars knew powerful arts and rebuilt a lion from bones. Their practical friend climbed a tree before they gave it life.
body: Four friends travelled together. Three were learned scholars with great technical knowledge. The fourth had little book learning but strong common sense.
They found bones in the forest. The scholars assembled them into a lion, gave it flesh, and prepared to give it life. The practical friend warned them, but they laughed.
He climbed a tree. The lion came alive and attacked the scholars. Knowledge without wisdom had created its own destroyer.
phal: Skill must be governed by consequence. Before asking whether we can, ask whether we should.
phalHi: कौशल को परिणाम-बुद्धि चाहिए। "कर सकते हैं" से पहले "करना चाहिए" पूछें।

title: The Hunter and the Pigeons
preview: A starving hunter was sheltered by a pigeon couple during a storm. Their compassion changed his heart more than fear ever could.
body: A hunter was caught in a storm and took shelter beneath a tree. In that tree lived a pigeon whose mate had been trapped by the same hunter.
Seeing the hunter cold and hungry, the pigeon still offered hospitality. He gathered dry leaves and lit a small fire for warmth.
The hunter was ashamed. The compassion of those he harmed opened his conscience. He freed the trapped bird and gave up cruelty.
phal: Compassion can awaken conscience where punishment only hardens fear.
phalHi: करुणा कई बार वह हृदय खोल देती है जिसे दंड नहीं खोल पाता।

title: The Raven and the Swan
preview: A raven mocked a swan for flying slowly. Over the ocean, the raven's tricks failed, and the swan's steady strength saved him.
body: A raven boasted of many styles of flying and mocked a swan for moving with calm simplicity. The swan invited him to cross the ocean.
At first the raven showed off: dipping, circling, and twisting in the air. But far from shore, he grew exhausted and began to fall.
The swan lifted him and carried him back. The raven learned that display is not endurance.
phal: Steady discipline outlasts flashy performance.
phalHi: दिखावा थोड़ी देर चमकता है; स्थिर अभ्यास दूर तक ले जाता है।

title: The Three Fish
preview: Three fish reacted differently to danger: one prepared early, one adapted quickly, and one denied the threat. Their choices decided their fate.
body: Three fish lived in a pond. When fishermen planned to return with nets, the first fish left through a channel that very night.
The second waited but stayed alert. When caught, he pretended to be dead and escaped when thrown aside. The third laughed at fear and did nothing.
The third was taken. The story remembers three responses to danger: preparation, adaptability, and denial.
phal: Prepare early when possible; adapt quickly when needed; never worship denial.
phalHi: संभव हो तो पहले तैयारी करें, आवश्यकता हो तो तुरंत उपाय करें, पर संकट से आँख न मूँदें।

title: Gold's Gloom
preview: A mouse grew strong and fearless while he lived above a hidden hoard of gold. When a clever guest dug up the treasure, the mouse lost all his strength overnight — and learned that his courage had never really been his own.
body: A mouse named Gold lived beneath a hermit's cell, feasting nightly on the leftovers the hermit hid away. However high the hermit hung his bowl, Gold leaped up to it with ease — a strength that amazed everyone who saw it.

One night a guest of the hermit noticed this and reasoned aloud: a creature does not gain such daring for no reason — he must be living near a hidden treasure, for the nearness of wealth alone can make the timid bold.

The guest and the hermit traced Gold's trail to his burrow and dug there, uncovering the very hoard of gold that Gold had been living above for years without ever knowing it consciously — only feeling its strange power.

The moment the gold was carried away, Gold tried his usual leap and fell flat on the floor. His own followers mocked him and deserted him, for they too had only respected the strength his nearness to wealth had given him.

Ashamed and powerless, Gold reflected through the night: it was never courage that had made him bold, only the comfort of gold nearby — and a creature who measures his own worth by his possessions will always be at the mercy of losing them.
In time Gold made peace with this truth. He stopped chasing the smell of treasure and found that real steadiness — the kind no one can dig up and carry away — comes only from within.
bodyHi: सोना नाम का एक चूहा एक साधु की कुटिया के नीचे रहता था और रोज़ रात साधु के बचे हुए भोजन पर गुज़ारा करता था। साधु भोजन का पात्र चाहे जितना ऊँचा टाँग दे, सोना बड़ी आसानी से उछलकर वहाँ पहुँच जाता था।
एक रात साधु के एक अतिथि ने यह देखा और कहा — बिना किसी कारण के कोई प्राणी इतना साहसी नहीं बनता; निश्चय ही वह किसी छिपे खज़ाने के पास रहता है, क्योंकि धन की निकटता ही डरपोक को भी निडर बना देती है।
अतिथि और साधु ने सोने के बिल तक उसका पीछा किया और वहाँ खोदा। उन्हें वही सोने का भंडार मिला जिसके ऊपर चूहा वर्षों से रहता आया था — बिना यह जाने कि उसकी शक्ति का असली स्रोत यही था।
जैसे ही सोना ले जाया गया, चूहे ने अपनी सामान्य छलांग लगाई पर औंधे मुँह गिर पड़ा। उसके साथी उसका मज़ाक उड़ाकर उसे छोड़ गए, क्योंकि वे भी उसकी शक्ति नहीं, केवल धन की निकटता का सम्मान करते थे।
लज्जित और शक्तिहीन सोना रातभर सोचता रहा — उसका साहस कभी उसका अपना नहीं था, केवल पास के धन की छाया थी। जो अपनी कीमत संपत्ति से आँकता है, वह उसे खोने पर हमेशा असहाय हो जाएगा।
समय के साथ सोने ने यह सच स्वीकार किया। उसने धन की गंध पीछा करना छोड़ दिया और पाया कि असली स्थिरता — जिसे कोई खोद कर नहीं ले जा सकता — केवल भीतर से आती है।
phal: Borrowed confidence — built on wealth, status, or possessions — vanishes the moment they are taken away. Only inner steadiness cannot be dug up and carried off.
phalHi: धन, पद या संपत्ति पर टिका उधार का आत्मविश्वास उनके छिनते ही मिट जाता है। केवल भीतर की स्थिरता ही ऐसी है जिसे कोई छीन नहीं सकता।

title: Mother Shandilee's Bargain
preview: A poor woman's sesame grain was spoiled by a stray dog. Rather than waste it, she offered a shrewd trade to a neighbor — hulled grain for unhulled. It looked like an ordinary bargain, but everyone who heard of it agreed: when Shandilee makes a deal, she always has a reason.
body: A poor Brahman's wife had set out sesame grain to dry in the sun after hulling it with great effort, meaning to feed a guest that evening as her husband had asked.

While she was occupied elsewhere, a stray dog fouled the grain. She could not bear to throw away what had cost her so much labor, so she thought of a plan: she would offer to trade her hulled grain, unhulled portion for portion, with any neighbor willing to exchange.

She went from door to door calling her offer, and a housewife nearby — glad to save the work of hulling — gladly traded her own raw, unhulled sesame for Shandilee's hulled grain, unaware of what had happened to it.

When Shandilee's husband later learned of the trade, he did not scold her for the small deception. Instead he grew thoughtful and said only this: whenever Mother Shandilee strikes a bargain that seems to favor her a little too easily, you may be certain she has good reason in her mind.
The saying spread beyond that household, becoming a gentle warning: a bargain that looks effortlessly generous is rarely without a hidden story — it pays to wonder why the other side is so willing.
bodyHi: एक गरीब ब्राह्मण की पत्नी ने बड़ी मेहनत से तिल छीलकर धूप में सुखाने रखा था, ताकि शाम को अतिथि को भोजन करा सके, जैसा उसके पति ने कहा था।
वह कहीं और व्यस्त थी तभी एक आवारा कुत्ते ने तिल गंदा कर दिया। इतनी मेहनत का तिल फेंकना उसे गवारा न हुआ, तो उसने एक उपाय सोचा — वह अपना छिला तिल किसी पड़ोसी के बिना छिले तिल से बदल लेगी।
वह घर-घर जाकर यह प्रस्ताव देने लगी, और एक पड़ोसन ने छीलने की मेहनत बचाने के लालच में खुशी-खुशी अपना कच्चा तिल उसके छिले तिल से बदल लिया, बिना यह जाने कि उस तिल के साथ क्या हुआ था।

जब शांडिली के पति को यह बात पता चली, तो उसने उसे डाँटा नहीं। बल्कि सोच में पड़कर बस इतना कहा — जब भी माँ शांडिली कोई सौदा करती है जो उसके पक्ष में बहुत आसानी से झुका लगे, समझ लो उसके मन में कोई कारण ज़रूर है।
यह कहावत घर से बाहर भी फैल गई, एक चेतावनी बनकर — जो सौदा बिना मेहनत के बहुत उदार लगे, उसके पीछे अक्सर कोई छिपी कहानी होती है; यह पूछना बुद्धिमानी है कि दूसरा पक्ष इतना तैयार क्यों है।
phal: When a deal looks unusually easy or one-sided in your favor, pause and ask why — shrewd people rarely give something for nothing.
phalHi: जब कोई सौदा असामान्य रूप से आसान या आपके पक्ष में झुका लगे, रुककर कारण पूछें — चतुर लोग बिना वजह कुछ नहीं देते।

title: Self-Defeating Forethought
preview: A starving jackal found a dead hunter and boar and planned to ration his feast carefully, starting with the bowstring. His caution cost him his life — a warning that even careful planning can turn deadly when greed guides it.
body: A hunter shot a great boar, but the wounded boar gored him fatally with his tusk before dying himself from the arrow. Both lay dead in the forest when a starving jackal wandered by and found this unexpected feast.

Delighted at his fortune, the jackal resolved to make the food last many days rather than gorge himself at once. He decided to begin with the sinew of the hunter's bow, nibbling it slowly and carefully, the way a wise man sips a rare elixir rather than gulping it down.
As he gnawed through the taut sinew at the bow's tip, the string suddenly snapped. The released bow-tip sprang up and pierced clean through the roof of his mouth.
The jackal died instantly from the very carefulness that was meant to preserve his fortune — his forethought about rationing had blinded him to the danger hidden in the very first bite.
The tale is remembered as a warning about greed dressed up as prudence: planning carefully to hoard more than you need can be more dangerous than simple hunger.
bodyHi: एक शिकारी ने एक विशाल सूअर पर तीर चलाया, पर मरते-मरते सूअर ने भी अपने दाँत से शिकारी को घातक घाव दे दिया। दोनों वन में मृत पड़े थे तभी एक भूखा सियार वहाँ से गुज़रा और यह अनपेक्षित भोज पाया।

अपने भाग्य से प्रसन्न सियार ने सोचा कि इस भोजन को एक साथ न खाकर कई दिनों तक बचा-बचा कर खाएगा। उसने पहले धनुष की डोरी से शुरू करने की सोची — धीरे-धीरे, जैसे बुद्धिमान मनुष्य दुर्लभ अमृत को घूँट-घूँट पीता है।
जब वह धनुष के सिरे पर बंधी तनी हुई डोरी चबा रहा था, डोरी अचानक टूट गई। छूटा हुआ धनुष का सिरा उछलकर उसके तालू को चीरता हुआ निकल गया।
सियार उसी सावधानी से मर गया जो उसने अपना भाग्य बचाने के लिए अपनाई थी — बचत की योजना ने उसे पहले ही कौर में छिपे खतरे से अंधा कर दिया था।
यह कथा एक चेतावनी के रूप में याद की जाती है — सावधानी का रूप धरा हुआ लालच, साधारण भूख से भी अधिक खतरनाक हो सकता है।
phal: Careful planning driven by greed is still greed — and it can be more dangerous than simple need, because caution disguises the risk until it is too late.
phalHi: लालच से प्रेरित सावधान योजना भी लालच ही है — और यह साधारण आवश्यकता से भी अधिक खतरनाक हो सकती है, क्योंकि सावधानी खतरे को तब तक छिपाए रखती है जब तक बहुत देर न हो जाए।

title: Mister Duly
preview: A young man spent a fortune on a book with a single line of wisdom and was disowned by his father. Repeating that one line through every strange turn of fortune, he eventually proved its truth: what is duly his, no one can take away — and what isn't his, no effort can keep.
body: A merchant's son once paid a hundred gold coins for an old book that contained only a single line: "What is duly his, a man receives." His furious father disowned him for such foolishness and threw him out of the house.

Wandering to a distant city, the young man became known only by that line, since he answered every question — his name, his home, his purpose — with the same words: "What is duly his, a man receives." People began calling him Mister Duly.

A chain of strange coincidences followed him: he wandered by mistake into a princess's chamber, then a policeman's house, then found himself in the wrong bed entirely, sleeping instead with a policeman's daughter who had mistaken him for her secret lover. Each time, when asked to explain himself, he simply repeated his one line — and each time, the person he'd confused sent him on his way, bewildered but unharmed.
At last, amid a runaway elephant's rampage through a wedding procession, Mister Duly alone stood his ground and calmly saved the terrified bride, driving the beast away while everyone else fled.

When the king himself arrived to sort out the extraordinary tangle of events, each woman he had encountered spoke up in turn, each finishing a line of the same old verse, until the truth emerged plainly. The king gave Mister Duly his daughter's hand and, having no son of his own, made him heir to the kingdom.

Through every twist — poverty, confusion, danger — nothing was ever truly lost or truly gained that was not already his by destiny. What is duly ours arrives in its own time; what is not ours slips away no matter how tightly we grasp it.
bodyHi: एक व्यापारी के पुत्र ने एक पुरानी किताब पर सौ स्वर्ण मुद्राएँ खर्च कीं, जिसमें केवल एक पंक्ति लिखी थी — "जो सचमुच उसका है, वह मनुष्य को अवश्य मिलता है।" क्रोधित पिता ने उसे इस मूर्खता के लिए घर से निकाल दिया।

दूर देश भटकते हुए युवक अपनी एक ही पंक्ति के लिए जाना जाने लगा, क्योंकि हर प्रश्न का — नाम, घर, उद्देश्य — वह वही उत्तर देता: "जो सचमुच उसका है, वह मनुष्य को अवश्य मिलता है।" लोग उसे "श्री यथोचित" कहने लगे।

कई अजीब संयोगों की श्रृंखला उसका पीछा करती रही — भूलवश वह एक राजकुमारी के कक्ष में, फिर एक सिपाही के घर, फिर गलत बिस्तर पर जा पहुँचा, जहाँ सिपाही की बेटी ने उसे अपना गुप्त प्रेमी समझ लिया। हर बार पूछे जाने पर वह वही पंक्ति दोहराता — और हर बार भ्रमित व्यक्ति उसे बिना हानि पहुँचाए विदा कर देता।
अंततः एक विवाह जुलूस में भागते हुए हाथी के बीच, जब सब भाग खड़े हुए, अकेला श्री यथोचित डटा रहा और शांतिपूर्वक भयभीत दुल्हन को बचाया, हाथी को खदेड़ दिया।

जब राजा स्वयं इस विचित्र उलझन को सुलझाने आए, तो हर स्त्री ने बारी-बारी उसी पुरानी पंक्ति का एक अंश जोड़ा, जब तक सच स्पष्ट न हो गया। राजा ने अपनी पुत्री का विवाह श्री यथोचित से कर दिया और निःसंतान होने के कारण उसे अपना उत्तराधिकारी बनाया।

हर मोड़ पर — दरिद्रता, भ्रम, खतरा — जो सचमुच उसकी नियति में नहीं था, वह कभी सच में मिला नहीं, और जो उसका था, वह कभी सच में छूटा नहीं। जो हमारा है, वह अपने समय पर आता है; जो हमारा नहीं, वह कसकर पकड़ने पर भी हाथ से निकल जाता है।
phal: What is truly meant for you arrives in its own time and cannot be lost; what isn't yours cannot be kept, however tightly you hold it.
phalHi: जो सचमुच आपके लिए नियत है, वह अपने समय पर आता है और खोया नहीं जा सकता; जो आपका नहीं, वह कसकर पकड़ने पर भी नहीं टिकता।

title: Soft the Weaver
preview: A weaver traveled far to earn a fortune, only to lose it mysteriously each time he returned home. Two unseen spirits — Doer and Deed — revealed that fate had capped his wealth at food and clothes alone. Granted one wish, he chose not more gold, but the freedom to give.
body: A weaver named Soft worked hard making fine garments, yet earned barely enough for food and clothes, while coarser weavers around him grew wealthy. Certain that a change of city would change his fortune, he set off for another land despite his wife's doubts about whether effort could really outrun destiny.

After three years he started home with three hundred gold coins, but slept one night beneath a banyan tree and overheard two spirits arguing in his dream — one called Doer, one called Deed. Deed insisted that Soft was fated to have nothing beyond food and clothes; Doer replied that he was only bound to reward effort, and the outcome afterward was Deed's affair. Soft woke to find his gold bag empty.
Undiscouraged, he earned five hundred gold coins the following year and took a different road home, only to find the very same tree, hear the very same argument, and wake to the very same empty bag.

In despair, he prepared to end his life beneath that tree — until one of the spirits appeared and stopped him, revealing himself as the very Deed who took the gold, and offering Soft one wish in place of his lost fortune.

Soft asked to understand wealth itself, and the spirit sent him to observe two merchants in the next city: one who hoarded everything fearfully and grew sick and friendless, and another who spent freely on gifts and hospitality and was rewarded by fortune again and again.

Watching this, Soft understood what he truly wanted — not a pile of gold he could never touch, but the freedom to give. He asked to become the kind of person whose money flows outward in generosity rather than locked away, and from that day his life found its true wealth.
bodyHi: कोमल नाम का एक जुलाहा मेहनत से सुंदर वस्त्र बुनता था, फिर भी बमुश्किल भोजन-वस्त्र जितना ही कमा पाता, जबकि मोटे कपड़े बुनने वाले धनी हो रहे थे। शहर बदलने से भाग्य बदलेगा, यह सोचकर वह पत्नी की शंका के बावजूद दूसरे देश चला गया।

तीन वर्ष बाद वह तीन सौ स्वर्ण मुद्राएँ लेकर लौटा, पर रास्ते में एक बरगद के नीचे सोते हुए सपने में दो आत्माओं — "कर्ता" और "कर्म" — को बहस करते सुना। कर्म ने कहा कि कोमल के भाग्य में केवल भोजन-वस्त्र लिखा है; कर्ता ने कहा कि वह केवल परिश्रम को पुरस्कार देने के लिए बाध्य है, आगे का परिणाम कर्म का विषय है। जागने पर उसकी थैली खाली थी।
निराश हुए बिना, अगले वर्ष उसने पाँच सौ स्वर्ण मुद्राएँ कमाईं और दूसरे रास्ते से लौटा, पर वही पेड़, वही बहस, और वही खाली थैली फिर मिली।
हताश होकर उसने उसी पेड़ के नीचे अपना जीवन समाप्त करने का निश्चय किया — तभी एक आत्मा प्रकट हुई, स्वयं को वही "कर्म" बताया जिसने धन लिया था, और खोए धन के बदले एक वरदान देने की पेशकश की।

कोमल ने धन का सच समझना चाहा, तो आत्मा ने उसे अगले शहर के दो व्यापारियों को देखने भेजा — एक जो सब कुछ डर-डरकर जमा करता था और रोगी व मित्रहीन हो गया, दूसरा जो खुले हाथ से दान-आतिथ्य करता और बार-बार भाग्य से पुरस्कृत होता।

यह देखकर कोमल ने समझा कि उसे वास्तव में क्या चाहिए — ऐसा धन नहीं जिसे वह छू भी न सके, बल्कि देने की स्वतंत्रता। उसने ऐसा बनने की कामना की जिसका धन उदारता में बहे, बंद न रहे — और उसी दिन से उसके जीवन को असली धन मिला।
phal: Wealth you cannot enjoy or share is no wealth at all. The freedom to give generously matters more than the size of what you hold.
phalHi: जिस धन का न उपभोग हो सके, न दान — वह धन नहीं। जो कुछ आपके पास है उसे उदारता से देने की स्वतंत्रता उसके आकार से अधिक मायने रखती है।

title: Hang-Ball and Greedy
preview: A jackal couple spotted odd folds of flesh hanging from a wild bull and were certain they would soon drop as an easy meal. The wife insisted they follow and wait. Fifteen years later, they were still waiting.
body: A powerful wild bull named Hang-Ball roamed the forest freely, and one day a jackal named Greedy and his wife noticed odd loose folds of flesh swinging beneath him as he walked to the river to drink.

The wife jackal was certain these folds would fall off any day, and urged her husband to abandon their comfortable spot — where mice came reliably to drink — and follow the bull instead, so as not to miss the coming feast.

Greedy doubted whether "someday" was worth giving up a sure thing today, but his wife pressed him with proverbs about boldness and effort, and reluctantly he agreed to follow the bull, telling himself the reward was surely close at hand.

Season after season, year after year, the couple trailed the bull, watching those same folds sway and never fall, growing thinner themselves as they lived on scraps instead of their old reliable mouse-trail.

In the fifteenth year, exhausted and no closer to their hoped-for feast, Greedy finally turned to his wife: whether these folds were loose or tight, falling or staying, they had watched them fifteen years for nothing — and it was time to go back to what had once fed them reliably.
The tale is remembered whenever someone chases a distant, uncertain windfall while abandoning something modest but sure — fifteen years is a long time to wait for a maybe.

title: Spot's Captivity
preview: A young fawn, not yet skilled at the herd's escape-leap, was caught by a hunter and raised as a prince's pampered pet. Yet no comfort could quiet his longing for the wild — until one monsoon night, a verse of homesickness set the whole palace in an uproar.
body: A young fawn named Spot, only six months old and still not skilled at the herd's special escape-leap that older deer used to clear hunters' snares, wandered too far ahead one day and was caught in a trap while the rest of the herd escaped to safety.

The hunter, moved by pity at the sight of so young a creature, spared his life and gave him as a gift to a prince, who kept Spot as a beloved pet — bathed, perfumed, fed delicacies, and passed fondly from hand to hand among the curious court.

Despite every comfort, Spot never stopped missing the wild herd he had lost. One night in the rainy season, hearing thunder and watching lightning, his heart grew so full of longing that he recited a verse aloud, asking when he would run with the herd again, bracing against the wind.
The prince, terrified to hear a voice from nowhere and thinking himself possessed by a demon, fled the room in disarray and offered a great reward to any healer who could cure him.
A wise man who happened to be present understood at once and gently explained: it was only the deer, aching with homesickness in the rainy season, that had spoken — not a demon at all.

Relieved and moved, the prince ordered Spot released back into the very forest he had come from. What looked like an unbreakable comfort could never replace the simple freedom of running with one's own kind.

title: The Four Treasure-Seekers
preview: Four poor Brahmans set out to find fortune. One by one, three stopped at copper, then silver, then gold — each thinking the next find must be better. Only the last kept going, straight into a curse that greed alone could not see coming.
body: Four Brahman friends, worn down by poverty, resolved to seek their fortune abroad. A wandering magician gave each of them a magic quill and told them to walk toward the Himalaya: wherever a man's quill dropped from his hand, treasure would be found beneath that very spot.

The first man's quill fell where the soil was pure copper. Satisfied, he filled his bag and turned back, content with what he had. Walking on, the second man's quill fell over silver — surely richer than copper — and he too turned home, pleased with his gain.

The third man's quill dropped over solid gold. His companion urged him onward, reasoning that if copper led to silver and silver to gold, something even greater must lie ahead. But the gold-finder had already found enough, and turned back satisfied, letting his friend go on alone.

The last man pressed on alone through the scorching land until he found not gems, as he had hoped, but a man imprisoned by a whirling wheel of torment, cursed to bear it forever — because he too had once asked the same greedy question the wrong way, without knowing when enough was enough.

The moment he asked, the wheel leapt from that stranger's head onto his own, and only then did he understand the price of chasing "just a little more" without limit. Each of the three earlier friends who stopped at copper, silver, or gold had unknowingly saved himself by recognizing when to be satisfied.

title: Hundred-Wit, Thousand-Wit, and Single-Wit
preview: Two clever fish, proud of their wit, stayed behind to outsmart the fishermen's nets. A humble frog with only one idea — leave now — survived them both. Cleverness that delays action is no match for a single decision made in time.
body: In a pond lived two fish named Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit, along with their friend, a frog named Single-Wit. One evening they overheard fishermen planning to return at dawn with nets, having judged the pond full of fish and shallow enough to sweep clean.

Alarmed, the frog asked his friends whether they should flee that very night. Thousand-Wit laughed off the danger, boasting that his thousand tricks would surely save them if trouble came. Hundred-Wit agreed, confident that a hundred clever schemes were more than enough for any crisis.
The frog admitted he had only a single idea, and it was simply to leave at once — so that night, he and his wife swam away to another pond, taking no chances.
At dawn the fishermen returned and swept the pond with their nets. Both clever fish, for all their boasted wit, were caught and carried away, struggling uselessly against the net until the end.

From the safety of his new home, the frog watched the fishermen pass by carrying his two brilliant friends, and said quietly to his wife that a single wit, acted on in time, had outlasted a thousand clever tricks that were never used.

title: The Musical Donkey
preview: A donkey and a jackal snuck into a farmer's field to feast on cucumbers. The donkey insisted on singing to celebrate the fine night, ignoring every warning. He got exactly the audience he asked for — just not the one he wanted.
body: A donkey and a jackal, friends by night, would slip through a gap in the hedge into a farmer's cucumber field and feast together, always parting before dawn to avoid trouble.

One fine night, the donkey — proud of his voice — announced that he wished to sing. The jackal begged him to stay quiet, reminding him that thieves, like lovers, do best to keep silent, and that his singing would only wake the farmers.
The donkey, offended at being called unmusical, launched into a long, proud explanation of the many rules and refinements of classical music, insisting he was far too cultured to be silenced.
The jackal, seeing there was no reasoning with him, quietly stepped away to keep watch instead — and the donkey brayed loudly across the field, exactly as the jackal had feared.

The farmers woke at once, rushed out with clubs, beat the donkey soundly, and fastened a heavy mortar around his neck before returning to sleep. As the battered donkey dragged himself away, the jackal called out with a smile: he had been offered fine advice and refused to take it — and now wore quite a "necklace" for his singing.

title: Slow the Weaver
preview: A weaver won a wish from a forest spirit. His friend urged him toward a kingdom, but his wife suggested something stranger: an extra head and pair of arms, to double his output. He got exactly what he asked for — and it cost him everything.
body: A weaver named Slow, needing wood for his broken loom, raised his axe against a great tree by the sea — only to discover it was home to a forest spirit, who begged him to spare it in exchange for any wish he desired.

Before deciding, Slow consulted his friend the barber, who urged him to ask for a kingdom, promising they would rule together. But Slow insisted on asking his wife too, despite the barber's warning that a woman's advice was not to be trusted.

His wife thought the barber's idea foolish and dangerous — a kingdom brings only worry and rivalry. Instead she suggested something that seemed cleverer: since one pair of hands already wove enough cloth to support them, an extra head and pair of arms would let him weave twice as much, doubling their income without any of a king's troubles.

Delighted with this "sensible" plan, Slow asked the spirit for exactly that — and instantly became two-headed and four-armed. But as he walked home rejoicing, the townspeople saw only a monstrous figure approaching and, terrified, beat him to death before he could explain himself.

What looked like the safer, more modest wish still proved fatal, because it was not the size of the request that mattered, but whether anyone had stopped to imagine how the world would actually receive it.
bodyHi: धीमा नाम के एक जुलाहे को अपने टूटे करघे के लिए लकड़ी चाहिए थी। उसने समुद्र किनारे एक विशाल पेड़ पर कुल्हाड़ी उठाई — तभी पता चला कि वह एक वनदेवी का घर है, जिसने पेड़ बचाने के बदले कोई भी इच्छा पूरी करने की पेशकश की।

निर्णय लेने से पहले धीमे ने अपने मित्र नाई से सलाह ली, जिसने राज्य माँगने को कहा, साथ राज करने का वादा किया। पर धीमे ने पत्नी से भी पूछने की ज़िद की, यद्यपि नाई ने चेताया कि स्त्री की सलाह पर भरोसा नहीं करना चाहिए।

पत्नी को नाई का विचार मूर्खतापूर्ण और खतरनाक लगा — राज्य केवल चिंता और प्रतिद्वंद्विता लाता है। इसके बजाय उसने कुछ अधिक समझदारी भरा सुझाव दिया — जब एक जोड़ी हाथ ही उनका गुज़ारा चला लेते हैं, तो एक अतिरिक्त सिर और भुजाएँ उसे दोगुना कपड़ा बुनने देंगी, बिना राजा की किसी मुसीबत के आय दोगुनी हो जाएगी।

इस "समझदार" योजना से प्रसन्न होकर धीमे ने वनदेवी से ठीक यही माँगा — और तुरंत दो सिर और चार भुजाओं वाला बन गया। पर घर लौटते हुए, खुशी से भरा, नगरवासियों ने केवल एक भयानक आकृति आते देखी और डरकर उसे पीट-पीटकर मार डाला, इससे पहले कि वह कुछ समझा पाता।
जो सुरक्षित, अधिक विनम्र इच्छा लगती थी, वह भी घातक साबित हुई — क्योंकि मायने माँग का आकार नहीं, बल्कि यह था कि किसी ने रुककर यह सोचा भी या नहीं कि दुनिया इसे वास्तव में कैसे देखेगी।
phal: A wish is only as wise as the thought given to how the world will actually receive it — modesty of ambition is not the same as wisdom of judgment.
phalHi: कोई इच्छा तभी बुद्धिमानी भरी होती है जब यह भी सोचा जाए कि दुनिया उसे वास्तव में कैसे लेगी — इच्छा की विनम्रता ही निर्णय की बुद्धिमत्ता नहीं है।

title: The Unforgiving Monkey
preview: A wise old monkey warned his troupe that a kitchen quarrel would end in disaster for them all. They laughed him off and paid dearly. The one who listened to himself and left survived — and made sure the injustice did not go unanswered.
body: A king kept a troupe of pet monkeys for his son's amusement, alongside a herd of rams. One greedy ram kept raiding the palace kitchen, and the cooks regularly drove him off with whatever came to hand.

The eldest monkey saw the danger this posed: if the cooks ever struck the woolly ram with a burning stick, he might catch fire, stampede into the nearby stable, and burn the horses too — and monkey-fat, he knew, was the prescribed remedy for burned horses in that land's medical texts. He urged the troupe to leave for the forest at once, but the others, comfortable with their palace treats, laughed at his fear and refused.

Unwilling to watch his family come to harm, the old monkey left alone for the forest. Soon after, exactly as he had feared, the burning ram fled into the stable, the horses were burned, and the king's physicians prescribed monkey-fat for the cure — so every monkey left behind was killed.

When the old monkey learned what had happened, he did not let the injustice pass quietly. He found a lake guarded by a man-eating spirit and struck a bargain: in exchange for a pearl necklace, he lured the same king and his retinue to the lake with tales of treasure, letting the spirit take them as they entered the water, while sparing the king himself with a final warning about what his cruelty had cost.

The tale is remembered for two lessons at once: that timely warnings deserve to be heeded before disaster, not after, and that injustice ignored does not simply disappear — it tends to return, in its own form, to the one who caused it.
bodyHi: एक राजा अपने पुत्र के मनोरंजन के लिए पालतू बंदरों का झुंड और मेढ़ों का एक समूह रखता था। एक लालची मेढ़ा बार-बार रसोई में घुस जाता, और रसोइए उसे जो मिले उससे भगा देते।

बुज़ुर्ग बंदर ने खतरा भाँप लिया — यदि कभी रसोइयों ने जलती लकड़ी से ऊनी मेढ़े को मारा, तो वह आग लगाकर अस्तबल में भाग सकता है, घोड़े जल सकते हैं — और उस देश के वैद्यक ग्रंथों में जले घोड़ों के इलाज के लिए बंदर की चर्बी बताई गई थी। उसने तुरंत वन जाने को कहा, पर बाकी बंदर, महल की सुविधाओं में लीन, उसका मज़ाक उड़ाकर मना कर गए।

अपने परिवार को खतरे में देखने से बेहतर, बुज़ुर्ग बंदर अकेला वन चला गया। जल्द ही, ठीक जैसा उसे डर था, जलता मेढ़ा अस्तबल में भाग गया, घोड़े जल गए, और राजवैद्यों ने इलाज के लिए बंदर की चर्बी बताई — सो पीछे रह गया हर बंदर मार डाला गया।

जब बुज़ुर्ग बंदर को यह पता चला, तो उसने अन्याय को चुपचाप जाने नहीं दिया। उसने एक नरभक्षी आत्मा से रक्षित झील खोजी और एक समझौता किया — मोतियों के हार के बदले, उसने राजा और उसके दरबारियों को खज़ाने की कहानी सुनाकर झील तक लुभाया, आत्मा को उन्हें पानी में लेने दिया, पर राजा को एक अंतिम चेतावनी देकर छोड़ दिया कि उसकी क्रूरता की कीमत क्या थी।

यह कथा दो सीख के लिए याद की जाती है — समय पर दी गई चेतावनी विपत्ति के बाद नहीं, पहले सुननी चाहिए; और अनदेखा किया गया अन्याय यूँ ही मिट नहीं जाता, वह किसी न किसी रूप में उसी के पास लौटता है जिसने उसे जन्म दिया।
phal: Timely warnings deserve to be heeded before disaster, not mourned after. Injustice ignored does not vanish — it tends to return to its source.
phalHi: समय पर दी गई चेतावनी विपत्ति के बाद पछतावे में नहीं, पहले ही सुननी चाहिए। अनदेखा किया गया अन्याय मिटता नहीं — वह अपने स्रोत की ओर लौट आता है।

title: The Credulous Fiend
preview: A water-spirit who devoured anyone who entered his lake overheard a princess mention a rival called "Twilight." Terrified of a threat that didn't exist, he fled from an ordinary horse-thief — and learned that fear born of rumor can make a fool of the mightiest creature.
body: A fiend haunted a princess every evening, unable to carry her off only because she protected herself with a magic circle. One night, overhearing her complain to a friend about "the one who torments me every evening at twilight," the fiend mistook this for the name of a rival — someone called Twilight, more powerful than himself.

Anxious to learn what this rival looked like, the fiend took the form of a horse and slipped into the royal stables to observe. That very night, a horse-thief crept in, chose the finest-looking horse — the disguised fiend — and rode off on him.

Every tug of the reins and crack of the whip convinced the terrified fiend that "Twilight" himself was punishing him. He bolted in panic, while the thief, equally alarmed that this horse obeyed no rein, clung on for dear life until he could grab a tree branch and escape.

A monkey friend of the fiend, watching from the branches, mocked him for running from his natural prey — a mere man — and the fiend, embarrassed, turned back to attack. But the thief, now furious rather than afraid, seized the monkey's dangling tail in his teeth and bit down hard, and the monkey — mistaking this for an even more terrifying force — froze in silent terror rather than uttering a sound.

Neither the fiend nor the monkey had faced anything more than an ordinary frightened man — but a single overheard word, misunderstood, had been enough to make each of them imagine a danger far greater than the truth.
bodyHi: एक भूत हर शाम राजकुमारी को तंग करता, पर उसे भगा नहीं पाता था क्योंकि वह जादुई घेरे से खुद को बचाती थी। एक रात, राजकुमारी को सहेली से "जो मुझे हर शाम संध्या के समय सताता है" कहते सुनकर, भूत ने इसे किसी प्रतिद्वंद्वी का नाम समझ लिया — "संध्या" नाम का, जो उससे भी शक्तिशाली हो।

यह प्रतिद्वंद्वी कैसा दिखता है यह जानने को उत्सुक, भूत ने घोड़े का रूप लेकर शाही अस्तबल में जगह ले ली। उसी रात एक घोड़ा-चोर वहाँ घुसा, सबसे बढ़िया दिखने वाले घोड़े — वेशधारी भूत — को चुना और भाग निकला।

लगाम की हर खिंचाई और चाबुक की हर आवाज़ भयभीत भूत को यकीन दिलाती रही कि स्वयं "संध्या" उसे दंड दे रहा है। वह घबराकर भागा, जबकि चोर, यह देखकर बराबर हैरान कि यह घोड़ा किसी लगाम को नहीं मानता, जान बचाने के लिए एक शाखा पकड़कर बच निकला।

शाखाओं से यह देख रहे भूत के मित्र बंदर ने उसका मज़ाक उड़ाया कि वह अपने स्वाभाविक शिकार — एक साधारण मनुष्य — से क्यों भाग रहा है, और शर्मिंदा भूत हमला करने पलटा। पर चोर, अब डरने के बजाय क्रोधित होकर, बंदर की लटकती पूँछ को दाँतों से जोर से पकड़ लिया, और बंदर — इसे और भी भयानक शक्ति समझकर — बिना आवाज़ किए भय से जड़ हो गया।
न भूत और न बंदर ने वास्तव में किसी साधारण डरे हुए मनुष्य से बढ़कर कुछ झेला था — पर एक अनसुनी, गलत समझी गई बात ही उन्हें असली खतरे से कहीं बड़ा डर कल्पना कराने के लिए काफी थी।
phal: Fear built on rumor and assumption, never checked against reality, can make even the mighty flee from nothing at all.
phalHi: अफ़वाह और अनुमान पर बना भय, जिसे कभी सच से परखा न जाए, शक्तिशाली को भी बिना किसी बात के भगा सकता है।

title: The Three-Breasted Princess
preview: A princess born with a rare mark that custom called a misfortune was married off to a blind beggar and exiled with him. A plot against his life, meant for harm, unraveled instead into an unexpected cure for everyone involved.
body: A king's newborn daughter carried a rare mark that the customs of the land considered a grave misfortune. His counselor advised consulting scholars rather than acting rashly, and they in turn ruled that she must be married off to whoever would have her — and both would then be exiled from the kingdom.

A drum was sounded announcing gold and a bride to anyone willing to marry her and leave. Eventually a blind man, guided everywhere by a hunchbacked companion, accepted the offer for the sake of the gold, reasoning that even hardship was better than the grinding poverty they already knew.

The three of them settled in a distant town. Over time, resentment grew between the hunchback and the princess against the blind man who depended so heavily on them, and the two of them began plotting to be rid of him for good.

Their scheme, meant to end in tragedy, unraveled instead in confusion: in the middle of carrying it out, the blind man's sight was accidentally restored by fumes he had not expected, and in the chaos and struggle that followed, the impact that was meant to harm him instead straightened the hunchback's back and smoothed away the very mark the princess had carried since birth.

What was set in motion as betrayal ended, by chance or by unseen justice, correcting every one of the misfortunes that had brought the three of them together in the first place — a reminder that outcomes rarely unfold exactly as those who plot them expect.
bodyHi: एक राजा की नवजात पुत्री एक दुर्लभ चिन्ह लेकर जन्मी, जिसे उस देश के रिवाज़ ने गंभीर अपशकुन माना। मंत्री ने जल्दबाज़ी में कदम उठाने के बजाय विद्वानों से सलाह लेने को कहा, और उन्होंने निर्णय दिया कि उसका विवाह किसी भी इच्छुक व्यक्ति से करके दोनों को राज्य से निर्वासित कर दिया जाए।

ढिंढोरा पिटवाया गया कि जो कोई उससे विवाह कर राज्य छोड़े, उसे सोना मिलेगा। अंततः एक अंधा व्यक्ति, जिसे हर जगह एक कुबड़ा साथी मार्गदर्शन देता था, सोने के लालच में यह प्रस्ताव स्वीकार कर लिया, यह सोचकर कि यह कठिनाई भी उनकी पहले की दरिद्रता से बेहतर होगी।
तीनों दूर के नगर में बस गए। समय के साथ, कुबड़े और राजकुमारी के मन में अंधे व्यक्ति के प्रति, जो उन पर इतना निर्भर था, नाराज़गी बढ़ने लगी, और दोनों ने उससे स्थायी रूप से छुटकारा पाने की साज़िश रची।

त्रासदी में समाप्त होने के लिए बनाई गई उनकी योजना उलझन में बदल गई — साज़िश को अंजाम देते समय, अप्रत्याशित धुएँ से अंधे व्यक्ति की दृष्टि लौट आई, और उसके बाद की उथल-पुथल में जो आघात उसे नुकसान पहुँचाने के लिए था, उसी ने कुबड़े की पीठ सीधी कर दी और राजकुमारी के जन्म-चिन्ह को मिटा दिया।

जो विश्वासघात के रूप में शुरू हुआ था, वह संयोग से या किसी अदृश्य न्याय से, उन तीनों को साथ लाने वाले हर दुर्भाग्य को ठीक करके समाप्त हुआ — यह याद दिलाते हुए कि परिणाम शायद ही कभी वैसे सामने आते हैं जैसे साज़िश रचने वाले सोचते हैं।
phal: Schemes meant to harm rarely unfold as their plotters expect — outcomes have a way of correcting themselves in ways no one can fully control.
phalHi: नुकसान पहुँचाने के लिए रची गई साज़िशें शायद ही वैसे सामने आती हैं जैसा साज़िशकर्ता सोचते हैं — परिणाम अक्सर ऐसे ढंग से सुधर जाते हैं जिसे कोई पूरी तरह नियंत्रित नहीं कर सकता।

title: The Fiend Who Washed His Feet
preview: A fiend captured a Brahman and carried him off — but a strange personal vow, meant to keep the fiend pure, became the very opening the Brahman needed to escape.
body: A fiend seized a Brahman in the forest, climbed onto his shoulders, and ordered him to walk on. As they went, the frightened Brahman noticed something strange: the fiend's feet were unusually soft, as though he took great care of them.

When asked why, the fiend explained that he was bound by a personal vow never to let his feet touch the ground unwashed. Soon they came to a lake, and the fiend told the Brahman to wait exactly where he stood while he went to bathe and complete his worship.

The Brahman understood at once what awaited him once the fiend returned satisfied from his ritual, and he also understood something else: bound by his own vow, the fiend would not dare set his unwashed feet on the ground to chase him.
